cues.text: Chapter two: OSI and TCP/IP.
When two devices communicate over a network, a lot of different jobs have to be done.
Bits must travel over a medium, frames must cross a local link, packets must be routed between networks, and applications must be able to understand each other.
To keep that complexity manageable, networking uses layered models.
Two matter most.
The OSI reference model separates network communication into seven layers.
TCP/IP is the practical Internet protocol suite, and it is usually presented as four layers, or as five when the physical layer is treated separately.
Let's walk through the seven OSI layers from the top down.
The table on screen shows three columns: the OSI layer, its main responsibility, and examples or the protocol data unit.
The protocol data unit is simply the name for the chunk of information handled at that layer.
Layer 7 is the Application layer.
Its responsibility is network services for applications.
Examples are HTTP, DNS and SMTP, and the unit is simply called data.
Layer 6 is the Presentation layer.
Its responsibility is representation, encoding, compression and encryption concepts.
In other words, it is about how data is represented and formatted so both sides interpret it the same way.
Examples are JSON and UTF-8, and the unit is again data.
Layer 5 is the Session layer.
Its responsibility is to establish and manage dialogue between communicating parties.
The example given is simply session concepts, and the unit is data.
Layer 4 is the Transport layer.
Its responsibility is end-to-end delivery, ports and reliability.
The units are TCP segments and UDP datagrams.
So at this layer, a TCP unit is called a segment and a UDP unit is called a datagram.
Layer 3 is the Network layer.
Its responsibility is logical addressing and routing.
The examples are IP packets and ICMP.
Here the unit is the packet.
Layer 2 is the Data link layer.
Its responsibility is local frames, MAC addressing and error detection.
Examples are Ethernet and 802.11 frames.
Here the unit is the frame, and 802.11 is the standard family used for wireless LANs.
Layer 1 is the Physical layer.
Its responsibility is signal and media transmission, and its unit is bits.
A handy way to remember the order, from seven down to one: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data link, Physical.
Now, how does the practical TCP/IP model line up with OSI?
Conceptually, the TCP/IP application layer covers OSI layers five to seven.
The TCP/IP transport layer corresponds to OSI layer four.
The internet layer corresponds to OSI layer three.
And the link, or network access, layer corresponds to OSI layers one and two.
One warning: protocols do not always fit a single OSI label.
TLS, for example, operates above transport, so it does not slot neatly into one numbered layer.
Since transport is where so much happens, let's look at the main transport protocols.
TCP provides ordered, reliable byte streams.
It does this with acknowledgments, sequence numbers and retransmission, and it also provides flow control and congestion control.
UDP, by contrast, provides connectionless datagrams without built-in reliable ordering.
That makes it useful for delay-sensitive traffic, or for applications that implement their own transport guarantees.
Finally, QUIC is built on UDP and offers reliable streams and encryption.
Next, encapsulation, which describes how data is wrapped as it moves down the layers.
The sequence is this.
The application message first becomes a transport header plus data.
Then an IP header is added to that segment.
Then a link header and trailer are added around the packet.
Finally, the result is sent as bits.
Decapsulation reverses this process at the receiving end, with each layer removing its own wrapping.
Some important behaviours follow from this.
Routers normally remove the incoming link frame and construct a new frame for the next hop.
IP addresses normally remain end-to-end, except with NAT or special tunnelling.
The TTL, or hop limit, decreases at each router.
And remember the division of labour: switches forward using MAC tables, while routers use IP routing tables.
Let's bring all this together with an example web request.
First, DNS resolves a name.
Then the host checks whether the destination is local, and resolves the next-hop MAC address if necessary.
Next, it establishes transport, which is TCP for typical HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2.
For HTTPS, it then authenticates and encrypts using TLS.
Only then does it send HTTP.
The receiving server processes the request and returns a response.
This sequence matters for troubleshooting, because a DNS failure, a route failure, a TLS certificate failure and an HTTP application error are different diagnostic layers.
Each points to a different place to look, so identifying which step failed tells you where to start fixing.
